body:
### What would you like to be added?

I propose for the introduction of Resource Size as a formal scalability dimension in Kubernetes. The scalability testing is still based on an 8 year old assumption that pods are simple, single-container applications with a minimal resource footprint (tested pods are ~4 KB). However, the evolution of Kubernetes, the rise of machine learning workloads, and the adoption of patterns like init containers and sidecars have led to significantly larger pod objects in real-world scenarios.

This discrepancy creates a significant friction point for users who unexpectedly encounter a hard scalability wall, where a cluster with as few as 50 nodes can become unstable with large pods, despite our official support for 5,000-node clusters.

Recent advancements in the API server ([blogpost](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/09/kubernetes-v1-34-snapshottable-api-server-cache/)), particularly in caching, response streaming, and API Priority and Fairness ([#132233](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/132233)), have substantially improved the control plane's ability to handle large resources . We are now in a strong position to formally address this gap, set an official goal for resource size scalability, and provide a more predictable experience for users running complex applications.

### Why is this needed?

When Kubernetes scalability goals were developed 7 years ago for the 1.6 release, the assumption was that most workloads would consist of simple, single-container applications. As a result, the size of the pod object itself was not considered a critical factor in scalability testing. Our official scalability tests for 5,000-node clusters still use pod objects of only 4 KB.

However, the Kubernetes ecosystem has evolved dramatically:
* Complex Application Architectures: Features like init containers, sidecars, and a growing number of environment variables have "supercharged" pod objects, making them much larger and more complex.
* Real-World Usage: We have observed that real-world pod sizes are often significantly larger than our tested scenarios, with pods averaging 10-20KB, and in some cases reaching even 100KB.
* A Surprising Scalability Cliff: While Kubernetes supports objects up to 1.5 MB, and our documentation states a 5,000-node scalability target, there is a practical, undocumented limit on pod size that users frequently and unexpectedly encounter. This leads to a poor user experience where they hit a hard scalability wall long before reaching documented limits for other dimensions like node or pod count.

The improvements in K8s 1.34 has shown that the API server can handle much larger resources efficiently. It's time to leverage these improvements to make resource size a first-class citizen in our scalability testing and guarantees.

## Proposed Plan

1. Enable Customization and Baseline Testing:
    * Add an option to customize resource size in our existing scalability tests.
    * Introduce a new, non-blocking scalability test with an increased resource size to establish a baseline and understand the current state of performance.
2. Document and Enforce:
    * Based on the initial findings, document the current realistic scalability threshold for resource size.
    * Promote the baseline test to be release-blocking to prevent regressions.
3. Iterate, Improve, and Decompose:
    * Begin a cycle of incrementally increasing the resource size in the non-blocking test.
    * With each increase, identify performance bottlenecks and address them.
    * As part of this process, develop component-specific benchmarks to isolate and analyze performance, similar to the ongoing work for LIST benchmarks ([#130169](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/130169)).
4. Define a Target:
    * Our proposed initial target is to **target support an average pod size of 100 KB** across our existing 150,000 pod scalability envelope. This goal represents only ~1/15th of the maximum object size supported,  making it resilient for large user application. At that level we expect the resource size will stop being concern for our users at all.
    * The initial target is soft goal that might be relaxed. The iterative nature of improvements should allow us to stop at any point, whether we encounter a hard blocker or reduction of active contributors.

By making resource size a formal dimension of our scalability envelope, we can provide a much more realistic and reliable experience for the Kubernetes community, ensuring that Kubernetes continues to be the best platform for running all types of workloads, from simple applications to complex, large-scale systems.

/sig scalability
/sig api-machinery 
/cc @wojtek-t @siyuanfoundation @liggitt @shyamjvs @marseel

comments.body: Big +1 for getting more realistic data to inform users of current state, and guide scale / performance fixes and investments
+1 - this is one of the dimensions that is most frequently hit by users nowadays; more methodological approach for investments is absolutely the way to go here

+1.

@serathius @wojtek-t I would be happy to help on this effort

To my understanding, we are currently defining scalability in terms of these [dimensions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md) .

Introducing this KEP will help positive side effects:
1. Will the thresholds in other dimensions also increase?
2. In the "define a target" section, you mentioned: 
> Our proposed initial target is to target support an average pod size of 100 KB across our existing 150,000 pod scalability envelope.

As per the dimension threshold, isn't it already at 150000?

3. What is exactly behind encapsulated behind the resource size that is not yet defined in the scalability envelope? Could you please clarify what resources are in this case are how do they differ with the existing enveloppe?
4. This KEP can also be a great proposal to have thresholds for current TBD scopes [ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/sig-scalability/configs-and-limits/thresholds.md). 

I'm happy to contribute to this in any ways.

What do you think? I would love to hear more about your thoughts on this.

First iteration of tests passed where I added 1KiB to the pod object. https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-scalability-gce#gce-master-scale-resource-size 

That increased the total resource size 705MiB to 871MiB. This can be observed via resource size metric in the scalability report https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-scale-resource-size/1979412375840755712/artifacts/GenericPrometheusQuery%20ResourceSize_load_2025-10-18T07:00:25Z.json

Let's start the process of increasing resource size until we get a failure.

Apart from in-tree use-cases, increased scalability would also be great for usecases where people build CRD-based systems to manage infrastructure and similar things through kubernetes-style controllers

Just seeing this, definitely echo the +1s. One thing I'll add to the above narrative, based on a recent exercise we did, is the cost of object writes. Reads, for good reasons, have been a big focus wrt size-based cost calculation so far ([xref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/request/list_work_estimator.go)), but it seems like standalone writes can also be substantially CPU hungry. Quick example: CPU usage on a 96 vcpu instance (correlated quite well with network in/out):

The ~12% CPU spike in between correlates specifically to these update calls for particular custom resource:

What's interesting is each of those writes executes quite fast (~20ms on avg): ``` apiserver_request_duration_seconds_sum{component="apiserver",dry_run="",group="core.humio.com",resource="humioclusters",scope="resource",subresource="status",verb="PUT",version="v1alpha1"} 132039.2143946648 apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{component="apiserver",dry_run="",group="core.humio.com",resource="humioclusters",scope="resource",subresource="status",verb="PUT",version="v1alpha1"} 5.923754e+06 ``` But they're issued back to back so their seat occupancy always stays low (almost 1 in this case):

And this is when there are no watches/lists on that resource type: ``` apiserver_longrunning_requests{component="apiserver",group="core.humio.com",resource="humioclusters",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="WATCH",version="v1alpha1"} 0 apiserver_request_duration_seconds_count{component="apiserver",dry_run="",group="core.humio.com",resource="humioclusters",scope="cluster",subresource="",verb="LIST",version="v1alpha1"} 0 ``` The average request size of the update call is ~25KB: ``` apiserver_request_body_size_bytes_sum{resource="humioclusters.core.humio.com",verb="update"} 1.38869154667e+11 apiserver_request_body_size_bytes_count{resource="humioclusters.core.humio.com",verb="update"} 5.922604e+06 ``` Yet to be dig deeper here if the cost comes mainly from object size or the fact that it's JSON. Either way, this shows it'll be useful to also benchmark writes without a lot of reads.

We have a passing test on 3GB of pod data https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-scale-resource-size/1996519952055537664 after the following changes (https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/35998, https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/36009)
* Increasing master size from n2-standard-32 to n2-standard-64, to accommodate master VM memory increase from 110GB to 140GB
* Increasing etcd quota to 20GB to fit more data
* Add requests for the exec-service pod used by clusterloader2 to connect to cluster network.
* Increase prow job memory from 16GB to 32GB

Next step: Incorporate a restart of master VM into the Load test scenario. This is meant to simulate scenarios like upgrades where controllers need to relist data from etcd. Without this controllers bootstrap just at the beginning and never relist.

Added the background informer that continuously re-lists pods. We went from 4 to 450 LIST request on pods. This also caused the LIST latency SLO to spike from 1s to 53s and test to start failing. I repeated the test with smaller resource which gave us maximum resource size of 2GB to fit within 30s. The main cause of high latency is GZIP encryption. As mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136030 using snappy can increase throughput by at least 2.5x. Based on that I will be proposing to allow clients/server to register custom compression algorithm. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136200

Important discovery related to large resources. Over half of the object size doesn't come from user inserted data. Instead it comes from ManagedFields metadata. Unfortunatelly this is by design https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/555-server-side-apply#scalability Example pod fields size analysis: To address it I'm proposing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137109 as a generic optimization, but also would be great if someone knowledgeable about SSA looks if there is anything that can be done on their side.

2 updates with not the greatest news.

The migration of scalability tests to Kops has negatively impacted our ability to support large resource size. I downsized the resource 2GB to 1.5GB and we still got a flake yesterday. Our hypothesis is fact that Kops runs addons (Prometheus, metrics server, exec-service etc) on control plane and interferes with components running there. @upodroid was working on fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kops/pull/17938, but progress stopped. This means there is a risk of making large resource tests release blocking for 1.36.

WatchList latency has been consistently worse than LIST latency, which is inconsistent with previous benchmarks https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3157#issuecomment-3737860792  cc @p0lyn0mial 
* [List latency for 1.5GB resource size](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=APIServer&metricname=LoadResponsiveness_PrometheusSimple&Resource=pods&Scope=cluster&Subresource=&Verb=LIST) is around 1s for P50, 14s for P90 and 29s for P99.
* [WatchList latency for 1.5GB resource size](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes-1.5GB-pods&metriccategoryname=APIServer&metricname=LoadResponsiveness_PrometheusSimple&Resource=pods&Scope=cluster&Subresource=&Verb=WATCHLIST) is around 2.4s for P50, 14s for P90, and 60+s for P99.

Would be good to investigate why so high P99 for WatchList, but I'm waiting for [improving tracing of streamed responses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136002). Without traces I can only guess. Need help with reviewing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137256 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137202
We got a first increase in release blocking test, went from 800MB to 1.5GB in release blocking tests https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/36400
Great Analysis of WatchList performance by @p0lyn0mial https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138327#issuecomment-4266114126
See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138415 for the next large step we are taking for this effort
